text: The ARACNE algorithm reconstructs gene regulatory networks from expression data using pairwise mutual information (MI). How does ARACNE distinguish direct regulatory edges from indirect ones (e.g., where A only affects C through an intermediate gene B)?
choices: It fits a random forest regression model that predicts each gene's expression from all other genes and uses feature importance as the edge weight
It applies the Data Processing Inequality: if A leads to B leads to C, then MI(A,C) is less than the minimum of MI(A,B) and MI(B,C), so the weakest edge of the resulting triangle is removed
It uses gradient boosting to rank candidate transcription-factor-target links roughly ten times faster than an equivalent regression-forest method
It Z-score normalizes each pair's mutual information against the background distribution of all pairs sharing one of the two genes
explanation: ARACNE's core principle is the Data Processing Inequality (DPI): for any indirect chain A to B to C, MI(A,C) cannot exceed the smaller of MI(A,B) and MI(B,C), so the weakest edge in each MI triangle is pruned as likely indirect. Choice 0 describes GENIE3 (random-forest regression), choice 2 describes GRNBoost2 (the gradient-boosting alternative used in SCENIC), and choice 3 describes CLR (Context Likelihood of Relatedness) -- all real but distinct GRN-inference methods from ARACNE.
